import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Oberwolfach problem

The Oberwolfach problem asks which $2$-regular graphs $G$ have the property that the complete graph
on the same vertex set decomposes into edge-disjoint copies of $G$. The conjectured classification
has four exceptional graphs, two of odd order and two of even order.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia: Oberwolfach problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberwolfach_problem)
- [Wikipedia: List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
-/

namespace OberwolfachProblem

open SimpleGraph

/--
The odd-order Oberwolfach problem: for every odd $n$ and every $2$-regular graph $G$ on $n$
vertices, $K_n$ decomposes into $(n-1)/2$ pairwise edge-disjoint copies of $G$ exactly when $G$
is neither $C_4 + C_5$ nor $C_3 + C_3 + C_5$.

The supremum condition says that the copies cover every edge of $K_n$; together with pairwise
disjoint edge sets, it says that every edge lies in exactly one copy. The canonical exceptional
graphs below use sum types to make their cycle components vertex-disjoint.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem oberwolfach_problem :
    ∀ (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)), Odd n → G.IsRegularOfDegree 2 →
      let twoTriangles :=
        fromRel (fun x y : Fin 2 × Fin 3 => x.1 = y.1 ∧ x.2 ≠ y.2)
      let fourFive :=
        (cycleGraph 4).map Function.Embedding.inl ⊔
          (cycleGraph 5).map Function.Embedding.inr
      let threeThreeFive :=
        twoTriangles.map Function.Embedding.inl ⊔
          (cycleGraph 5).map Function.Embedding.inr
      (∃ copies : Fin ((n - 1) / 2) → SimpleGraph (Fin n),
          (∀ i, Nonempty (G ≃g copies i)) ∧
          Pairwise (fun i j => Disjoint (copies i).edgeSet (copies j).edgeSet) ∧
          ⨆ i, copies i = completeGraph (Fin n)) ↔
        ¬(Nonempty (G ≃g fourFive) ∨ Nonempty (G ≃g threeThreeFive)) := by
  sorry

/--
The even-order extension of the Oberwolfach problem: for every even $n$ and every $2$-regular
graph $G$ on $n$ vertices, the graph obtained from $K_n$ by deleting a perfect matching decomposes
into $n/2-1$ pairwise edge-disjoint copies of $G$ exactly when $G$ is neither $C_3+C_3$ nor
$C_3+C_3+C_3+C_3$.

The perfect matching is existentially quantified; all perfect matchings of a complete graph are
equivalent by symmetry. The supremum and pairwise-disjointness conditions say that every edge
outside the matching lies in exactly one copy.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem oberwolfach_problem.variants.even :
    ∀ (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)), Even n → G.IsRegularOfDegree 2 →
      let twoTriangles :=
        fromRel (fun x y : Fin 2 × Fin 3 => x.1 = y.1 ∧ x.2 ≠ y.2)
      let fourTriangles :=
        fromRel (fun x y : Fin 4 × Fin 3 => x.1 = y.1 ∧ x.2 ≠ y.2)
      (∃ matching : (completeGraph (Fin n)).Subgraph,
          matching.IsPerfectMatching ∧
          ∃ copies : Fin (n / 2 - 1) → SimpleGraph (Fin n),
            (∀ i, Nonempty (G ≃g copies i)) ∧
            Pairwise (fun i j => Disjoint (copies i).edgeSet (copies j).edgeSet) ∧
            ⨆ i, copies i = (completeGraph (Fin n)).deleteEdges matching.edgeSet) ↔
        ¬(Nonempty (G ≃g twoTriangles) ∨ Nonempty (G ≃g fourTriangles)) := by
  sorry

end OberwolfachProblem
modeling_decisions: Formalized the article's widely believed classification as an iff: solvability holds exactly outside the listed exceptional isomorphism classes. This includes the known nonexistence direction for the exceptions and the open existence direction for all other instances.

Represented an edge decomposition by an indexed family of simple graphs, each isomorphic to the given graph, whose edge sets are pairwise disjoint and whose supremum is the host graph. The index types enforce exactly (n-1)/2 copies in odd order and n/2-1 copies in even order.
Used graphs on Fin n, so the complete host and the given 2-regular graph have exactly the same n vertices. The hypotheses Odd n and Even n separate the original and extended formulations.

Represented C4+C5 and C3+C3+C5 by mapping their components into sum types and taking graph supremums. Represented repeated disjoint triangles by the canonical graph on Fin k × Fin 3 whose vertices are adjacent exactly when they lie in the same block and are distinct.

For the even variant, existentially quantified a perfect-matching subgraph of the complete graph and decomposed the result of deleting its edge set. This matches the source; the choice of matching is immaterial by symmetry.
Used Mathlib's finite simple-graph 2-regularity. Consequently all components are cycles of length at least three, as required, and degenerate small orders cannot satisfy the regularity hypothesis.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# The Oberwolfach problem

The Oberwolfach problem asks which finite $2$-regular graphs $G$ admit a decomposition of the
complete graph on the same vertices into copies of $G$. For odd order, it is conjectured that the
only exceptions are $C_4 + C_5$ and $C_3 + C_3 + C_5$. The even-order extension removes a perfect
matching from the complete graph; its conjectured exceptions are two and four disjoint triangles.

*Reference:* [Wikipedia, Oberwolfach problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberwolfach_problem)
-/

namespace OberwolfachProblem

open SimpleGraph

/-- A graph `H` has a decomposition indexed by `ι` into copies of `G` if its edges are partitioned
by graphs on the same vertex type, each isomorphic to `G`. -/
def HasCopyDecomposition {V ι : Type*} (H G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃ c : ι → SimpleGraph V, H.IsEdgeColouring c ∧ ∀ i, Nonempty (G ≃g c i)

/--
**Oberwolfach problem, odd order.** Let $G$ be a $2$-regular graph on an odd number $n$ of
vertices. The complete graph $K_n$ can be decomposed into $(n-1)/2$ edge-disjoint copies of $G$
if and only if $G$ is neither $C_4+C_5$ nor $C_3+C_3+C_5$. Thus every edge of $K_n$ occurs in
exactly one copy. Here all cycle lengths are at least three, as the graphs are simple.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem oberwolfach_problem (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) (hn : Odd n)
    (hG : G.IsRegularOfDegree 2) :
    HasCopyDecomposition (ι := Fin ((n - 1) / 2)) (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) G ↔
      ¬ Nonempty (G ≃g cycleGraph 4 ⊕g cycleGraph 5) ∧
      ¬ Nonempty (G ≃g (cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3) ⊕g cycleGraph 5) := by
  sorry

/--
**Even-order Oberwolfach problem.** Let $G$ be a $2$-regular graph on an even number $n$ of
vertices. There is a perfect matching $M$ such that $K_n-M$ can be decomposed into $n/2-1$
edge-disjoint copies of $G$ if and only if $G$ is neither two nor four disjoint triangles.
Every edge outside $M$ occurs in exactly one copy. The choice of $M$ is immaterial up to a
symmetry of $K_n$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem oberwolfach_problem.variants.even (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) (hn : Even n)
    (hG : G.IsRegularOfDegree 2) :
    (∃ M : (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin n)).Subgraph, M.IsPerfectMatching ∧
      HasCopyDecomposition (ι := Fin (n / 2 - 1))
        ((⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) \ M.spanningCoe) G) ↔
      ¬ Nonempty (G ≃g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3) ∧
      ¬ Nonempty
        (G ≃g ((cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3) ⊕g cycleGraph 3) ⊕g cycleGraph 3) := by
  sorry

end OberwolfachProblem

Interpreted the article's open-ended question using its stated widely believed classification: solvability is equivalent to not being graph-isomorphic to the listed exceptional disjoint unions of cycle graphs.
Represented the complete graph by `⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin n)` and a decomposition into copies by an edge partition whose classes are each graph-isomorphic to the given graph.
Indexed the odd decomposition by `Fin ((n - 1) / 2)` and the even decomposition by `Fin (n / 2 - 1)`, as forced by edge counts.

For the even variant, existentially quantified a `Subgraph` of the complete graph satisfying `IsPerfectMatching` and decomposed the graph difference by its `spanningCoe`; this follows the source, and the particular matching is immaterial by complete-graph symmetry.
Encoded each exceptional graph directly with Mathlib's `cycleGraph` and disjoint graph sum `⊕g`, and used `Nonempty` graph isomorphisms so vertex labels and sum associativity choices are irrelevant.
Did not impose a separate cycle-length bound: on a finite simple graph, degree exactly two yields disjoint cycle components, necessarily of length at least three.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Oberwolfach problem

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Oberwolfach problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberwolfach_problem)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [arxiv/1806.04644](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.04644)
  S. Glock, F. Joos, J. Kim, D. Kühn, D. Osthus, *Resolution of the Oberwolfach problem*,
  J. Eur. Math. Soc. 23 (2021).

The Oberwolfach problem, posed by Ringel in 1967, asks which $2$-regular graphs $G$ have the
property that the complete graph on the same number of vertices can be decomposed into
edge-disjoint copies of $G$. In Ringel's formulation, $n$ conference participants are to be seated
at round tables of prescribed sizes (adding up to $n$) for several meals, so that every two
participants sit next to each other exactly once.

A $2$-regular graph is a disjoint union of cycles $C_x + C_y + C_z + \cdots$ (of lengths
$\ge 3$), and the corresponding instance of the problem is denoted $OP(x, y, z, \ldots)$.
Glock, Joos, Kim, Kühn and Osthus proved that all but finitely many instances have a solution,
and all instances with $n \le 60$ have been settled. The only instances known to have no solution
are $OP(3, 3)$, $OP(3, 3, 3, 3)$, $OP(4, 5)$ and $OP(3, 3, 5)$, and it is widely believed that
every other instance has a solution.
-/

namespace OberwolfachProblem

open SimpleGraph

variable {V : Type*}

/--
A simple graph `H` on the vertex type `V` *decomposes into copies of* a simple graph `G` on `V`
if `H` is the union of a set of pairwise edge-disjoint graphs on `V`, each isomorphic to `G`.
Equivalently, every edge of `H` lies in exactly one of the copies.
-/
def DecomposesIntoCopiesOf (H G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃ S : Set (SimpleGraph V), (∀ H' ∈ S, Nonempty (H' ≃g G)) ∧
    S.Pairwise (fun H₁ H₂ => Disjoint H₁.edgeSet H₂.edgeSet) ∧ sSup S = H

/-- Every graph decomposes into a single copy of itself. -/
@[category API, AMS 5]
lemma decomposesIntoCopiesOf_self (G : SimpleGraph V) : DecomposesIntoCopiesOf G G := by
  refine ⟨{G}, ?_, Set.pairwise_singleton _ _, sSup_singleton⟩
  rintro H' (rfl : H' = G)
  exact ⟨Iso.refl⟩

/-- Only the edgeless graph decomposes into copies of the edgeless graph. -/
@[category API, AMS 5]
lemma decomposesIntoCopiesOf_bot_iff (H : SimpleGraph V) :
    DecomposesIntoCopiesOf H ⊥ ↔ H = ⊥ := by
  refine ⟨?_, fun h => h ▸ decomposesIntoCopiesOf_self _⟩
  rintro ⟨S, hS, -, hH⟩
  rw [← hH, sSup_eq_bot]
  intro H' hH'
  obtain ⟨e⟩ := hS H' hH'
  ext u v
  simpa using e.map_rel_iff.symm.mp

/-- The instance $OP(3)$ has a solution: $K_3$ is a single copy of the triangle $C_3$. -/
@[category test, AMS 5]
lemma op_three : DecomposesIntoCopiesOf (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin 3)) (cycleGraph 3) := by
  rw [cycleGraph_three_eq_top]
  exact decomposesIntoCopiesOf_self _

/--
**The Oberwolfach problem** (Ringel, 1967). Let $G$ be a $2$-regular graph on $n$ vertices, i.e. a
disjoint union of cycles $C_x + C_y + C_z + \cdots$ of lengths $x, y, z, \ldots \ge 3$ with
$x + y + z + \cdots = n$; this instance is denoted $OP(x, y, z, \ldots)$. Which such $G$ have the
property that the complete graph $K_n$ on the same number of vertices can be decomposed into
edge-disjoint copies of $G$, i.e. every edge of $K_n$ lies in exactly one copy?

A decomposition can only exist when $n$ is odd (each copy of $G$ uses two of the $n - 1$ edges at
every vertex), and then it consists of $(n - 1)/2$ copies of $G$. It is known that $OP(4, 5)$ and
$OP(3, 3, 5)$ have no solution, and it is widely believed that every other instance has one.
The statement below is this conjectured answer: for odd $n$, $K_n$ decomposes into copies of $G$
if and only if $G$ is isomorphic neither to $C_4 + C_5$ nor to $C_3 + C_3 + C_5$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem oberwolfach_problem [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hG : G.IsRegularOfDegree 2) (hV : Odd (Fintype.card V)) :
    DecomposesIntoCopiesOf (⊤ : SimpleGraph V) G ↔
      IsEmpty (G ≃g cycleGraph 4 ⊕g cycleGraph 5) ∧
      IsEmpty (G ≃g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 5) := by
  sorry

/--
**The Oberwolfach problem for even $n$** (Huang, Kotzig and Rosa, 1979). Let $G$ be a
$2$-regular graph on an even number $n$ of vertices. Then $K_n$ itself cannot be decomposed into
copies of $G$, and one asks instead whether all of the edges of $K_n$ except for a perfect
matching $I$ can be covered by edge-disjoint copies of $G$, i.e. whether $K_n - I$ decomposes
into $n/2 - 1$ copies of $G$. (By the symmetry of $K_n$, the choice of $I$ is immaterial.)
It is known that $OP(3, 3)$ and $OP(3, 3, 3, 3)$ have no solution, and it is widely believed
that every other even instance has one. The statement below is this conjectured answer: for
even $n$, $K_n - I$ decomposes into copies of $G$ if and only if $G$ is isomorphic neither to
$C_3 + C_3$ nor to $C_3 + C_3 + C_3 + C_3$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem oberwolfach_problem.variants.even [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hG : G.IsRegularOfDegree 2) (hV : Even (Fintype.card V)) :
    (∃ M : (⊤ : SimpleGraph V).Subgraph, M.IsPerfectMatching ∧
      DecomposesIntoCopiesOf ((⊤ : SimpleGraph V) \ M.spanningCoe) G) ↔
      IsEmpty (G ≃g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3) ∧
      IsEmpty (G ≃g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3) := by
  sorry

end OberwolfachProblem

One remark: the second slot's text ('covered by copies') could in isolation be read as allowing overlaps, but the article's diner reformulation ('exactly once') and the cited literature make the intended meaning an edge-disjoint decomposition, as the slot notes say; the file follows the notes.
modeling_decisions: The list-page statement is an open-ended 'which' question. Following the decomposition notes and the article ('widely believed that all other instances have a solution'), each slot is stated as the conjectured characterization in iff form: decomposable ↔ G is not one of the known exceptions. The → direction (the exceptions are unsolvable) is known by computer search; the ← direction is the open part. An alternative would be `{...} = answer(sorry)` over a set of graphs; the explicit iff was chosen because the notes say 'except exactly' and prescribe the candidate answer.

Oddness of n is a hypothesis `Odd (Fintype.card V)` for the main slot rather than part of the answer (the literature poses the problem 'for which (odd) n and F'). Without it the iff would be false for even n (LHS false, RHS true), so the hypothesis is required for the iff form. The even case is the separate variant slot with hypothesis `Even (Fintype.card V)`.

The 2-regular graph G is taken on an arbitrary finite vertex type V, and K_n is `⊤ : SimpleGraph V` (same vertex set, hence 'the same number of vertices'). A 'copy' of G is a graph on V isomorphic to G (`Nonempty (H' ≃g G)`); since |V(G)| = n, copies are automatically spanning and this coincides with images of G under vertex embeddings.

'Decomposed into edge-disjoint copies' is formalized as: a set S of graphs on V, each isomorphic to G, pairwise edge-disjoint (`Set.Pairwise` on `Disjoint ·.edgeSet ·.edgeSet`), whose lattice supremum `sSup S` equals the target graph. Hence every edge lies in exactly one copy. The number of copies ((n-1)/2, resp. n/2-1) is not imposed since it is forced; a set rather than an indexed family is used because two distinct copies of a graph with edges cannot coincide.

In the even variant, the article's word 'covered' is read as an edge-disjoint decomposition (each edge exactly once), following the article's own diner formulation ('next to each other diner except their own spouse exactly once') and the cited papers ('decomposition of K_n minus a perfect matching into n/2 - 1 copies').

The removed perfect matching is quantified existentially (`∃ M : (⊤ : SimpleGraph V).Subgraph, M.IsPerfectMatching ∧ ...`), matching the text 'except for a perfect matching'; by the symmetry of K_n this is equivalent to the universal version. K_n − I is written `(⊤ : SimpleGraph V) \ M.spanningCoe`.

Exceptional graphs are written with Mathlib's `cycleGraph k : SimpleGraph (Fin k)` and the disjoint sum `⊕g` (e.g. `cycleGraph 4 ⊕g cycleGraph 5` for OP(4,5)); 'G is not this graph' is `IsEmpty (G ≃g ...)`, i.e. non-isomorphism.

Degenerate inputs: n = 1, 2 admit no 2-regular graph (vacuous); n = 0 (empty V, even) makes both sides of the even variant true (empty decomposition of the empty graph, empty perfect matching), so no spurious falsity is introduced. `[Fintype V] [DecidableRel G.Adj]` are used only so that `IsRegularOfDegree` (which needs `LocallyFinite`) typechecks.

/--
**The Oberwolfach problem** (Ringel, 1967). Let $G$ be a $2$-regular graph on $n$ vertices, i.e. a
disjoint union of cycles $C_x + C_y + C_z + \cdots$ of lengths $x, y, z, \ldots \ge 3$ with
$x + y + z + \cdots = n$; this instance is denoted $OP(x, y, z, \ldots)$. Which such $G$ have the
property that the complete graph $K_n$ on the same number of vertices can be decomposed into
edge-disjoint copies of $G$, i.e. every edge of $K_n$ lies in exactly one copy?

A decomposition can only exist when $n$ is odd (each copy of $G$ uses two of the $n - 1$ edges at
every vertex), and then it consists of $(n - 1)/2$ copies of $G$. It is known that $OP(4, 5)$ and
$OP(3, 3, 5)$ have no solution, and it is widely believed that every other instance has one.
The statement below is this conjectured answer: for odd $n$, $K_n$ decomposes into copies of $G$
if and only if $G$ is isomorphic neither to $C_4 + C_5$ nor to $C_3 + C_3 + C_5$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem oberwolfach_problem [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hG : G.IsRegularOfDegree 2) (hV : Odd (Fintype.card V)) :
    DecomposesIntoCopiesOf (⊤ : SimpleGraph V) G ↔
      IsEmpty (G ≃g cycleGraph 4 ⊕g cycleGraph 5) ∧
      IsEmpty (G ≃g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 5) := by
  sorry

$2$-regular graph on an even number $n$ of vertices. Then $K_n$ itself cannot be decomposed into
copies of $G$, and one asks instead whether all of the edges of $K_n$ except for a perfect
matching $I$ can be covered by edge-disjoint copies of $G$, i.e. whether $K_n - I$ decomposes
into $n/2 - 1$ copies of $G$. (By the symmetry of $K_n$, the choice of $I$ is immaterial.)
It is known that $OP(3, 3)$ and $OP(3, 3, 3, 3)$ have no solution, and it is widely believed
that every other even instance has one. The statement below is this conjectured answer: for
even $n$, $K_n - I$ decomposes into copies of $G$ if and only if $G$ is isomorphic neither to
$C_3 + C_3$ nor to $C_3 + C_3 + C_3 + C_3$.
-/

    (hG : G.IsRegularOfDegree 2) (hV : Even (Fintype.card V)) :
    (∃ M : (⊤ : SimpleGraph V).Subgraph, M.IsPerfectMatching ∧

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Oberwolfach problem

The Oberwolfach problem, posed by Ringel in 1967, asks which $2$-regular graphs $G$ have the
property that the complete graph on the same number of vertices can be decomposed into
edge-disjoint copies of $G$. A $2$-regular graph is a disjoint union of cycles
$C_x + C_y + C_z + \cdots$ (each of length at least $3$), and the corresponding instance of the
problem is denoted $OP(x, y, z, \ldots)$.

If $G$ has $n$ vertices, a decomposition of $K_n$ into copies of $G$ can only exist when $n$ is
odd, since every vertex of $K_n$ has degree $n - 1$ and every copy of $G$ contributes $2$ to it.
The problem has also been extended to even $n$ by asking whether $K_n$ minus a perfect matching
can be decomposed into copies of $G$.

It is known that $OP(3, 3)$, $OP(3, 3, 3, 3)$, $OP(4, 5)$ and $OP(3, 3, 5)$ have no solution,
and it is widely believed that every other instance has a solution. Glock, Joos, Kim, Kühn and
Osthus proved that all but finitely many instances have a solution.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberwolfach_problem)
- [Wikipedia: List of unsolved problems in
  mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [GJKKO21] S. Glock, F. Joos, J. Kim, D. Kühn, D. Osthus, *Resolution of the Oberwolfach
  problem*, J. Eur. Math. Soc. 23 (2021), 2511–2547.
  [arXiv:1806.04644](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.04644)
- [SDTBD19] F. Salassa, G. Dragotto, T. Traetta, M. Buratti, F. Della Croce, *Merging
  Combinatorial Design and Optimization: the Oberwolfach Problem*.
  [arXiv:1903.12112](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.12112)
- [DFHMR10] A. Deza, F. Franek, W. Hua, M. Meszka, A. Rosa, *Solutions to the Oberwolfach
  problem for orders 18 to 40*, J. Combin. Math. Combin. Comput. 74 (2010), 95–102.
-/

namespace OberwolfachProblem

open SimpleGraph

variable {V W : Type*}

/--
The graph `H` *decomposes into edge-disjoint copies of* `G` if there is a finite set `S` of
injective vertex maps `f : V ↪ W` such that the copies `G.map f` (`f ∈ S`) have pairwise
disjoint edge sets and their union is `H`. Equivalently, every edge of `H` lies in exactly one
copy of `G`.
-/
def DecomposesIntoCopies (H : SimpleGraph W) (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃ S : Finset (V ↪ W),
    (S : Set (V ↪ W)).PairwiseDisjoint (fun f => (G.map f).edgeSet) ∧ ⨆ f ∈ S, G.map f = H

/-- Every graph decomposes into a single copy of itself. -/
@[category test, AMS 5]
theorem decomposesIntoCopies_self (G : SimpleGraph V) : DecomposesIntoCopies G G :=
  ⟨{Function.Embedding.refl V}, by simp, by simp⟩

/-- The instance $OP(3)$ has a solution: $K_3$ is a single copy of $C_3$. -/
@[category test, AMS 5]
theorem decomposesIntoCopies_top_cycleGraph_three :
    DecomposesIntoCopies (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin 3)) (cycleGraph 3) :=
  ⟨{Function.Embedding.refl (Fin 3)}, by simp, by
    simp only [Finset.iSup_singleton, map_id, SimpleGraph.ext_iff, funext_iff]
    decide⟩

/--
**The Oberwolfach problem.** Let $G$ be a $2$-regular graph on $n$ vertices, with $n$ odd (for
even $n$ the complete graph $K_n$ has odd degree, so no decomposition into $2$-regular graphs can
exist). Then $K_n$ decomposes into edge-disjoint copies of $G$ if and only if $G$ is not one of
the two exceptional graphs $C_4 + C_5$ (the instance $OP(4, 5)$, $n = 9$) and
$C_3 + C_3 + C_5$ (the instance $OP(3, 3, 5)$, $n = 11$).

The two exceptions are known to have no solution [DFHMR10]; the open part is the claim that
every other instance has a solution, which is widely believed and is proved for all sufficiently
large $n$ in [GJKKO21].
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem oberwolfach_problem [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hG : G.IsRegularOfDegree 2) (hV : Odd (Fintype.card V)) :
    DecomposesIntoCopies (⊤ : SimpleGraph V) G ↔
      IsEmpty (G ≃g cycleGraph 4 ⊕g cycleGraph 5) ∧
        IsEmpty (G ≃g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 5) := by
  sorry

/--
**The Oberwolfach problem for even $n$.** Let $G$ be a $2$-regular graph on $n$ vertices, with
$n$ even. Then there is a perfect matching $I$ of $K_n$ such that $K_n - I$ (the complete graph
with the edges of $I$ removed) decomposes into edge-disjoint copies of $G$ if and only if $G$ is
not one of the two exceptional graphs $C_3 + C_3$ (the instance $OP(3, 3)$, $n = 6$) and
$C_3 + C_3 + C_3 + C_3$ (the instance $OP(3, 3, 3, 3)$, $n = 12$).

Since the automorphism group of $K_n$ acts transitively on perfect matchings, it does not matter
which perfect matching is removed. The two exceptions are known to have no solution; the open
part is the claim that every other instance has a solution, which is widely believed and is
proved for all sufficiently large $n$ in [GJKKO21].
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem oberwolfach_problem.variants.even [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hG : G.IsRegularOfDegree 2) (hV : Even (Fintype.card V)) :
    (∃ I : (⊤ : SimpleGraph V).Subgraph, I.IsPerfectMatching ∧
        DecomposesIntoCopies (⊤ \ I.spanningCoe) G) ↔
      IsEmpty (G ≃g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3) ∧
        IsEmpty (G ≃g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3) := by
  sorry

end OberwolfachProblem
attempts.decomposition_objections: None. The table's reading (exceptions C_4 + C_5 and C_3 + C_3 + C_5 for odd n; OP(3^2), OP(3^4) for even n; removed perfect matching immaterial by symmetry) agrees with the article and the cited GJKKO paper and was followed.
modeling_decisions: The list-page entry is an open-ended 'which 2-regular graphs' question. Following the decomposition table notes and the article's 'Known results' (exceptions OP(3^2), OP(3^4), OP(4,5), OP(3,3,5) are unsolvable and 'it is widely believed that all other instances have a solution'), each slot is stated as the widely believed complete characterization: solvable ↔ G is not one of the exceptional graphs. The ← direction is the open conjecture; the → direction (the exceptions are unsolvable) is a known result. No answer(sorry) is used, because the answer set is a class of graphs up to isomorphism and cannot be expressed as a simple set equation.

Odd n is a hypothesis of oberwolfach_problem (as in Glock–Joos–Kim–Kühn–Osthus: 'for which (odd) n and F'), rather than being folded into the right-hand side. Without it the iff is false (e.g. C_4 on K_4), since K_n with n even has odd degree.

'Copies of G' are the images G.map f for injective vertex maps f : V ↪ V; since V is finite these are bijections, so each copy is a spanning isomorphic image of G in K_n, matching the seating interpretation. The number of copies is not fixed to (n-1)/2 (resp. n/2 - 1); it is forced by edge counting, so this is equivalent.

Edge-disjointness is required in both slots ('decomposed into edge-disjoint copies'; in the even variant the article says 'covered' but the cited literature asks for a decomposition into n/2 - 1 copies, which forces edge-disjointness by edge counting).

Even variant: the perfect matching I is existentially quantified ('all edges except for a perfect matching'), as a Subgraph of ⊤ with Subgraph.IsPerfectMatching, and the target graph is ⊤ \ I.spanningCoe. By vertex-transitivity of K_n on perfect matchings this is equivalent to quantifying universally.

The exceptional graphs are written concretely as SimpleGraph.sum (⊕g) of Mathlib's cycleGraph, e.g. cycleGraph 4 ⊕g cycleGraph 5 on Fin 4 ⊕ Fin 5, and 'G is not an exception' is IsEmpty (G ≃g …). Cycle lengths ≥ 3 are automatic for 2-regular simple graphs.
[DecidableRel G.Adj] is assumed so that G.IsRegularOfDegree 2 (which needs LocallyFinite) elaborates; this is a harmless local Decidable instance.

Boundary cases checked: n = 0 is excluded from the odd slot; in the even slot V empty makes both sides true (empty matching, empty decomposition, no isomorphism with a 6- or 12-vertex graph), so no false statement arises; n = 1, 2 admit no 2-regular graphs.

/-!
# Oberwolfach problem

The Oberwolfach problem asks which disjoint unions of cycles decompose a complete graph on the
same vertices into isomorphic copies. For even order, one first removes a perfect matching.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Oberwolfach problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberwolfach_problem)
-/

namespace OberwolfachProblem

open SimpleGraph

/--
The proposed answer to the Oberwolfach problem for odd order is that every 2-regular graph `G`
on at least three vertices decomposes the complete graph into `(n - 1) / 2` edge-disjoint copies
of `G`, except exactly for $C_4 + C_5$ and $C_3 + C_3 + C_5$. Here `IsEdgeColouring` says that
the copies cover every edge exactly once.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem oberwolfach_problem {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hcard : 3 ≤ Fintype.card V) (hodd : Odd (Fintype.card V))
    (hregular : G.IsRegularOfDegree 2) :
    (∃ copies : Fin ((Fintype.card V - 1) / 2) → SimpleGraph V,
        (completeGraph V).IsEdgeColouring copies ∧
          ∀ i, Nonempty (G ≃g copies i)) ↔
      ¬ Nonempty (G ≃g cycleGraph 4 ⊕g cycleGraph 5) ∧
      ¬ Nonempty (G ≃g (cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3) ⊕g cycleGraph 5) := by
  sorry

/--
The proposed answer to the even-order extension is that, after deleting a perfect matching from
the complete graph, every 2-regular graph `G` on at least three vertices decomposes the remaining
graph into `n / 2 - 1` edge-disjoint copies of `G`, except exactly for $C_3 + C_3$ and
$C_3 + C_3 + C_3 + C_3$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem oberwolfach_problem.variants.even {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V)
    [DecidableRel G.Adj] (hcard : 3 ≤ Fintype.card V) (heven : Even (Fintype.card V))
    (hregular : G.IsRegularOfDegree 2) :
    (∃ M : (completeGraph V).Subgraph, M.IsPerfectMatching ∧
      ∃ copies : Fin (Fintype.card V / 2 - 1) → SimpleGraph V,
        ((completeGraph V) \ M.spanningCoe).IsEdgeColouring copies ∧
          ∀ i, Nonempty (G ≃g copies i)) ↔
      ¬ Nonempty (G ≃g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3) ∧
      ¬ Nonempty
        (G ≃g ((cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3) ⊕g cycleGraph 3) ⊕g cycleGraph 3) := by
  sorry

end OberwolfachProblem
modeling_decisions: Interpreted the open-ended “which” question using the candidate exact classification stated in the background article: all admissible 2-regular graphs except the two listed odd-order exceptions, expressed as an equivalence.

Represented a decomposition by a family of spanning simple graphs indexed by the required number of copies, using `SimpleGraph.IsEdgeColouring` for exact edge coverage and pairwise edge-disjointness, and `SimpleGraph.Iso` to require every member to be a copy of the given graph.

Represented each exceptional disjoint union explicitly with Mathlib's `SimpleGraph.cycleGraph` and graph disjoint sum `⊕g`. For finite simple 2-regular graphs on at least three vertices, components are cycles of length at least three.

For the even variant, existentially quantified a `Subgraph` of the complete graph satisfying Mathlib's `IsPerfectMatching`, deleted its spanning edge graph, and decomposed the remainder. This follows the source; which perfect matching is selected is immaterial by complete-graph symmetry.

Included `3 ≤ Fintype.card V` to exclude the vacuous empty graph from Lean's pointwise definition of 2-regularity and to reflect that the source's cycle components have length at least three. Together with parity this gives order at least 3 in the odd case and at least 4 in the even case.

Included `DecidableRel G.Adj` only as computational typeclass data needed by Mathlib's finite-degree API; every graph on a finite vertex type has such an instance classically, so it does not impose an additional mathematical restriction.

Following CONTRIBUTING's preferred style for questions and the precedent `Wikipedia/SumOfThreeCubes.lean`, each slot is stated as `answer(sorry) ↔ (∀ …, property ↔ conjectured characterization)`, where the characterization is the article's candidate answer ('It is known that for OP(3^2), OP(3^4), OP(4,5), and OP(3,3,5) no solution is possible and it is widely believed that all other instances have a solution'). `answer(True)` = the conjectured characterization is correct.

Both slots use a two-sided `↔` between 'the decomposition exists' and 'G is not one of the exceptional graphs'. The `←` direction is the open conjecture; the `→` direction (the four exceptional instances have no solution) is the established fact recorded by the article and the cited papers (Deza–Franek–Hua–Meszka–Rosa 2010; Glock–Joos–Kim–Kühn–Osthus). This is what 'which graphs' asks for; a reviewer should confirm they want the full characterization rather than only the existence direction.

The 2-regular graph is quantified as `G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)` with `G.IsRegularOfDegree 2` (a `[DecidableRel G.Adj]` instance binder is included only so that `degree` is defined; the statement does not depend on the instance). 'Cycles of length ≥ 3' is automatic for simple graphs.

The parity restriction is a hypothesis (`Odd n` for the main slot, `Even n` for the variant), matching the article ('must be an odd number') and the table notes ('necessarily n odd'). Putting `Odd n` inside the characterization instead would be false at n = 0 (the empty graph is vacuously 2-regular and vacuously decomposes), so the hypothesis form is the safe faithful one. Boundary cases checked: n = 0 (even slot: both sides true, consistent), n = 1, 2 (no 2-regular graph, vacuous), n = 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9 agree with known results.

The number of copies is fixed explicitly as `(n - 1) / 2` (odd) and `n / 2 - 1` (even), as in the table notes and the cited papers; this count is forced by edge counting whenever a decomposition exists, so it adds no extra constraint.

The exceptional graphs are written concretely as `cycleGraph 4 ⊕g cycleGraph 5`, `cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 5`, `cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3`, and `cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3` (Mathlib `cycleGraph k` is C_k for k ≥ 3; `⊕g` is the disjoint sum), compared with `G` via `Nonempty (G ≃g …)`. statement_blocks.oberwolfach_problem:
/--
**The Oberwolfach problem.** Which $2$-regular graphs $G$ have the property that the complete
graph $K_n$ on the same number $n$ of vertices can be decomposed into edge-disjoint copies
of $G$?

Since every vertex of $G$ has degree $2$ and every vertex of $K_n$ has degree $n - 1$, a
decomposition can only exist when $n$ is odd, and then it consists of exactly $(n-1)/2$ copies
of $G$. It is known that the two instances $OP(4, 5)$ (i.e. $G = C_4 + C_5$, $n = 9$) and
$OP(3, 3, 5)$ (i.e. $G = C_3 + C_3 + C_5$, $n = 11$) have no solution, and it is widely
believed that all other instances have a solution. The conjectured answer is therefore:
for odd $n$, a $2$-regular graph $G$ on $n$ vertices has the property if and only if $G$ is
not isomorphic to $C_4 + C_5$ or to $C_3 + C_3 + C_5$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem oberwolfach_problem :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ (n : ℕ), Odd n → ∀ (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) [DecidableRel G.Adj],
      G.IsRegularOfDegree 2 →
      (DecomposesInto (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) ((n - 1) / 2) G ↔
        ¬ (Nonempty (G ≃g cycleGraph 4 ⊕g cycleGraph 5) ∨
          Nonempty (G ≃g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 5))) := by
  sorry
